Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Indigenous Lands & Innovation' — Indigenous nations using technology, governance, and stewardship on their own terms.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-9: geopolitical and war news with no Indigenous rights angle; general wildfire and wildlife-service updates not led by or directly affecting Indigenous communities or guardians; provincial forestry and environmental policy with no explicit First Nations involvement; consumer tech and gadget reviews; science with no Indigenous stewardship or sovereignty context; crime and judicial news unrelated to Indigenous rights.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. Indigenous-led journalism on governance, rights, and self-determination is a strong fit on its own: a technology hook raises a score but is NOT required to reach the top band.
- 80-100: Excellent Indigenous-led reporting. Cariboo stories bridging governance or culture AND technology land here (Tŝilhqot'in/Secwépemc/Dakelh language revitalization tech, guardian programs using sensors and drones, GIS land mapping, Indigenous-led connectivity, digital heritage projects) — and so does outstanding national coverage of sovereignty, treaty, and land rights.
- 55-79: Solid pan-Canadian Indigenous governance, sovereignty, land rights, treaty, or reconciliation journalism — APTN, Eagle Feather News, or IndigiNews-style coverage of First Nations governance, MMIWG, land claims, self-determination, and Indigenous-led services. Most Indigenous governance journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Indigenous cultural, community, or human-interest stories (awards, events, ceremonies) with limited governance substance, or BC land-stewardship and environmental stories with meaningful First Nations involvement.
- 10-29: General BC land, environmental, or forestry stories that mention Indigenous communities only in passing.

The British Columbia Conservation Officer Service said forensic evidence linked a female grizzly and her three yearling cubs to the deaths. The bears were killed, and investigators believe the attack likely involved rare predatory behaviour. Elected Chief Tlhmtimut Samuel Schooner said community support services would remain available for as long as needed. The Nuxalk Nation thanked conservation officers for resolving the incident, while saying the deaths had reopened trauma from the previous attack. Authorities also confirmed the four bears were not involved in that earlier attack, which injured 11 people.

Heavy rain and flooding across British Columbia’s South Coast prompted shelter-in-place advisories near Squamish and in Pemberton Valley, while evacuation orders covered parts of Pemberton and Lil’wat Nation on Thursday, Nov. 12. Some areas received more than 300 millimetres of rain in 48 hours, and floodwater closed Highway 99 east of Pemberton and roads near Squamish. The entire Village of Pemberton was under an evacuation alert. Evacuation orders also remained in effect in Zeballos, where flooding and landslide risks threatened about 30 properties. items.title: [winnipegfreepress.com] Ottawa drops appeal of Alberta ruling on federal project review law
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Canada’s federal government will not appeal an Alberta Court of Appeal ruling that parts of the Impact Assessment Act exceed federal authority and says it will amend the law to address the ruling. The court ruled in October that the legislation could let Ottawa block a project under provincial jurisdiction based on even a minimal effect in an area of federal jurisdiction. Ottawa has not announced the details or timing of the amendments. They are expected to be developed alongside Bill C-39, now before Parliament, which would shorten project reviews and shift assessments of pipelines, power lines and some nuclear and uranium projects to specialist regulators.

items.title: [japantimes.co.jp] Climate change intensified Indonesia’s worst wildfires in a decade, study finds
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

A World Weather Attribution study published Friday found that a strong El Niño drove Indonesia’s severe rainfall shortfall this year, while human-caused climate change made temperatures during the August-to-October fire season about 1.6 degrees Celsius higher. Researchers said warming made hot, dry fire conditions about three times more likely, while El Niño cut seasonal rainfall by roughly half. Decades of deforestation and peatland drainage also left the landscape more vulnerable to ignition. The fires have spread hazardous haze across Indonesia and neighboring Southeast Asian countries. Nusantara Atlas, an independent monitoring platform, estimated that fires affected 2.88 million hectares from January through October. The Indonesian government had not confirmed that total or issued its own estimate. Researchers called for peatland restoration, stronger land protections and reduced fossil-fuel emissions. Fires were still burning, with smoke detected in eastern Kalimantan on Nov. 12.

items.title: [rabble.ca] Canadians rally nationwide against bill expanding fast-track project powers
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

More than 65 protests took place across Canada on Nov. 12 against Bill C-39, the federal Building Canada Strong Act, which would let Cabinet designate regions of “national interest” and accelerate approvals for major projects. The bill could cover pipelines, energy infrastructure and industrial developments and would set a one-year timeline for decisions on designated projects. Indigenous, environmental and labour groups argue the bill could weaken environmental safeguards, treaty rights and workers’ ability to strike; the federal government says it would speed up projects supporting economic growth and energy security while maintaining Indigenous consultation. A House of Commons committee is studying the bill, and a special Senate committee is conducting a pre-study; no date for its final House vote has been publicly announced.

The researchers say these regions help regulate Earth’s energy, water and carbon cycles, and their decline increases the risks of sea-level rise, ecosystem damage and flooding. The team assessed four indicators against conditions over the past 11,700 years, when a relatively stable climate allowed human civilizations to develop. The researchers say the findings support urgent cuts to greenhouse-gas emissions and call for limits on black carbon and local disturbances such as industrial expansion. The authors released the paper during the COP31 climate conference and urged policymakers to use the proposed boundaries in climate planning.

Amnesty International said South Sudanese authorities and the United Nations Mission in South Sudan (UNMISS) failed to act on advance warnings before armed men attacked Abiemnom on March 1, killing at least 213 people. In a report released Nov. 12, the rights group said 1,000 to 1,500 men from Mayom County carried out a four-hour assault, burning homes and attacking part of the local hospital. The death toll reported by South Sudanese authorities included 130 residents, 76 security personnel and seven foreign nationals. Amnesty said authorities and UNMISS had received warnings of a possible attack about two weeks earlier, and that around 1,000 residents sought refuge at a UNMISS base in the 48 hours before the assault. It called for an independent investigation, accountability for those responsible and a public review of the mission’s response. UNMISS said it focused its limited capacity on people sheltering at its base and sent 40 additional police personnel after the attack.

items.title: [cisa.gov] U.S. agencies warn hackers are targeting industrial refrigeration controls
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Five U.S. agencies warned on Nov. 5 that hackers are targeting industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems worldwide, including controllers used by grocery stores, hospitals, food producers and transport operators. Attackers may exploit unpatched or internet-accessible devices to change temperatures or defrost settings, or prevent operators from seeing temperature readings. Such attacks could spoil stock, compromise storage safety and damage equipment. The warning follows attacks on European supermarkets on Nov. 2 and an incident that altered refrigeration settings at three French blood-service facilities. The U.S. agencies did not say whether refrigeration systems in the United States had been targeted. They urged operators to remove unnecessary internet access, secure remote connections, update firmware, isolate control systems from business networks and set alerts for unsafe temperature changes.

items.title: [bleepingcomputer.com] Attack on French blood-service contractor reaches refrigeration controls
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

An attack on a refrigeration service provider used by France’s national blood service reached monitoring and control systems at three sites on Nov. 2. The blood service said it was not directly targeted. Investigators have not publicly identified how attackers entered the contractor’s systems, which control equipment was affected or who was responsible. French reporting said attackers set controls to request temperatures as high as 110°C, but that figure does not establish the temperatures reached inside storage units or blood products. European retailers have also faced attacks on internet-connected refrigeration controls. Interface cybersecurity adviser Sven Herpig said the supermarket attacks exploited weak or known credentials and a lack of multi-factor authentication, while another security expert pointed to default passwords and outdated systems. Investigators have not confirmed that the blood-storage attack exploited the same weaknesses or was linked to the retail incidents. The European Commission, the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) and other EU bodies advised organizations to act immediately to reduce exposure and are sharing information with national authorities. Under the EU Cyber Resilience Act, manufacturers have been required to report severe incidents and actively exploited vulnerabilities since Sept. 11, 2026. Its main security requirements take effect Dec. 11, 2027.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot condemned the decision and said France would continue to work for a two-state solution. France’s presidential election is scheduled for April 18 and May 2, 2027.

items.title: [stpetersburg.usf.edu] Study finds drought could cut cactus habitat by 80% by 2100
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

An international research team analyzed nearly 1,000 cactus species and found that more than a quarter could lose at least 80% of their suitable habitat by 2100 if severe droughts intensify. The researchers added drought projections to climate models, which commonly use long-term temperature and rainfall averages, and combined them with biodiversity records, field observations and community-science data. The projected losses could qualify affected species as Critically Endangered under criteria set by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), more than doubling the number of cacti in that category. Researchers say drought may also reduce growth or flowering without immediately killing plants, compounding threats from habitat destruction and illegal collection. The findings are expected to inform updated IUCN Red List assessments; the team says further research is needed to determine which life stages and biological processes drought affects.

items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Cattle advisers and researchers are urging producers to match winter rations to forage quality and herd needs. Drought has tightened forage supplies, and feed is a major operating expense. South Dakota State University research found that limit-fed, energy-dense diets reduced feed use and methane emissions without harming calf growth through weaning, saving about $29 per cow. Kansas State University cow-calf specialist Jason Warner recommends assessing forage and supplementing protein as dormant grasses lose quality. French livestock trainer Guillaume Beaure describes reducing feed waste by closely matching rations to animals’ needs. Advisers also recommend checking forage mineral levels because winter hay can pose a risk of magnesium deficiency.

items.title: [spravy.stvr.sk] AI data-center developers plan 181 GW of fossil-fuel power plants
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Developers are proposing 181 gigawatts of fossil-fuel power plants beside planned AI data centers in the United States, Britain and continental Europe to avoid lengthy grid-connection delays, according to research firm BloombergNEF. If built, about 90% of the plants would be in the United States and produce an estimated 345 million metric tons of carbon-dioxide equivalent annually. BloombergNEF forecasts that AI data-center electricity demand will reach 2,354 terawatt-hours by 2035, nearly four times current levels and about 7% of global electricity use. Data-center electricity demand is growing faster than grid capacity, while households are covering part of the infrastructure costs. In the United States, data-center electricity demand has risen 19% a year since 2020, while grid capacity has expanded 2% annually. A separate estimate found that data centers covered only 38% of the $8.25 billion in grid costs associated with their growth in 2025, leaving residents to pay most of the remainder.

items.title: [arstechnica.com] FAA plans to replace floppy-based air traffic systems by 2028
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

The Federal Aviation Administration plans to replace four aging information systems that rely on floppy disks with a unified digital platform at 435 air traffic facilities by the end of 2028. The new Enterprise Information Display System, or E-IDS, will consolidate weather alerts, airport status and flight notices that controllers currently retrieve through outdated, often manual processes. The FAA says the platform will give controllers faster access to safety-critical information and reduce maintenance problems. The agency has already upgraded five sites, while Congress has provided $12.5 billion for broader air traffic control modernization. The FAA is seeking additional funding through the proposed Modern Skies Act. The agency plans to deploy the system at the remaining locations by the end of 2028.

items.title: [theguardian.com] UN-backed report warns overshooting 1.5C could permanently damage Earth's ice
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

A report by 80 scientists convened by the International Cryosphere Climate Initiative and the U.N. Environment Programme warns that even a temporary rise above the Paris Agreement’s 1.5C warming limit could cause lasting losses to glaciers, sea ice and polar ice sheets. Earth has already warmed about 1.3C from preindustrial levels. The authors say any period above 1.5C should be as brief as possible before temperatures fall much further, and identify a long-term target below 1C by 2150. Under current policies, warming is projected to reach about 2.8C, a level the report links to near-total thaw of near-surface permafrost and likely severe disruption to ocean circulation. Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets would continue losing ice even if temperatures later returned to 1.5C, while many ice systems could take centuries or millennia to recover. The report was released ahead of the COP31 climate conference in Turkey.

items.title: [thehackernews.com] Hackers use 4,837 hijacked GitHub accounts to steal continuous integration secrets
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

A campaign dubbed wfx-loot used stolen credentials from 4,837 GitHub accounts to probe more than 61,000 repositories and plant code designed to steal developer and cloud secrets. Security researchers confirmed the payload ran in at least 1,806 repositories. A separate analysis counted malicious commits in 8,093 public repositories, but that does not mean the code executed in each one. The attackers tested access with pull requests titled “docs: dependency audit notes,” then briefly inserted a roughly 1,500-line script into GitHub Actions workflows or npm installation hooks. The script sought GitHub, cloud, package-publishing and AI-service credentials. Attackers often reverted the changes and deleted workflow logs. The campaign relied on valid stolen account tokens, not a flaw in GitHub Actions. Researchers said the operation was still active on Nov. 12, with new probe requests and malicious code still appearing. They advised repository owners to revoke compromised access, rotate every secret available to affected workflows and check cloud accounts for persistent access.

Security researchers found that 35,578 of 37,571 web apps built with SpaceXSI’s Grok Build, a chat-based app builder, were accessible without signing in, exposing business and personal information at SpaceXSI and 30 other organizations. Claroc, the security firm that found the apps, estimated that about one in 10 accessible apps contained internal or personal data and roughly 2% held material it rated high or critical in severity. Exposed material included a SpaceXSI sales map covering 594 strategic accounts, a hospital directory listing more than 3,500 employees, an intensive-care briefing about a patient and a timesheet with 18 users’ passwords in its code. The apps’ addresses were discoverable through searchable passive DNS records, and Grok Build preselected “Anyone with the link” as the sharing option in the researchers’ test. SpaceXSI removed 24 apps made by its own staff and X employees; Claroc said other users’ apps remained available and that it had begun contacting affected organizations.

items.title: [al-monitor.com] US sanctions eight Canadian currency firms over alleged Iran transfers
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

The U.S. Treasury on Nov. 6 sanctioned eight money-services businesses in Ontario and British Columbia, alleging they moved funds for Iran and sanctioned Iranian entities, including by converting Iranian rials and other currencies into digital assets. The businesses are Million Exchange, Amin Exchange, Top PC Technician, NIA Nations Currency, Farah Exchange, CCC Inc., Cryptoyal and Darvish Exchange. The sanctions block any assets they hold under U.S. jurisdiction and bar U.S. persons and entities from transacting with them. U.S. officials also said several firms handled money for Ryan Wedding, a Canadian former Olympic snowboarder and alleged drug-trafficking figure. The Treasury accused three firms of laundering drug proceeds by converting bulk cash into digital assets. The action was coordinated with the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC), Canada’s financial intelligence agency, and U.S. agencies. Separately, the Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), the U.S. anti-money-laundering unit, barred U.S. financial institutions from processing transfers involving MEXC Global, a cryptocurrency exchanger incorporated in Seychelles. FinCEN said MEXC facilitated at least $16 billion in illicit transactions linked to Iran, North Korea and Russia, as well as other sanctioned actors.

items.title: [scimex.org] Astronomers trace eight-minute radio pulses to white dwarf and Sun-like star
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Astronomers have traced repeating radio pulses from the system GPM J071507−114153 to a white dwarf orbiting a Sun-like star—the first known long-period radio transient with this type of stellar pairing. The pulses recur every 7.9 minutes but appear only during a roughly six-hour window in each 32-hour orbit. The system lies more than 5,000 light-years away. Researchers discovered the system using Australia’s Murchison Widefield Array, pinpointed it with South Africa’s MeerKAT telescope and used the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii to identify the companion as a G-type star. Measurements of the orbit and the companion’s slight movement indicate that the pulsing object has about two-thirds the Sun’s mass, making it too light to be a neutron star. The study was published in Nature Astronomy on Nov. 12, 2026.

items.title: [yna.co.kr] Doctors file complaint with UN rights experts over police hospital search
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Three South Korean medical groups have filed an urgent complaint with United Nations human rights experts over a police search of a pediatric emergency center at Ajou University Hospital, saying the operation threatened patients’ right to life and doctors’ rights. Police conducted the search on Sept. 30 while investigating a child patient’s death. The Korean Medical Association is also holding a series of solo protests and demanding a police apology and safeguards against repeat searches. It says legal authorization alone does not address possible disruption to emergency treatment. The groups asked the U.N. to seek an explanation of the search’s legal basis and recommend changes to South Korea’s investigative guidelines. They also said they plan to contact international medical and human rights organizations.

On Friday, coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki said air defenses destroyed two ballistic missiles launched toward Najran. Debris fell, and authorities began assessing damage. The coalition also reported intercepting drones in the Makkah and Riyadh regions. The Houthis have repeatedly denied targeting Makkah or Madinah and say their operations target oil infrastructure and military sites. The latest interceptions follow the breakdown of a truce in July and renewed fighting in Yemen, where government forces have sought to retake territory from the Houthis.
